fixes.explanation: The edge of the field isn't where the verse puts him. Shammah "…took his stand in the middle of the field…" (2 Samuel 23:12). Israel's troops had fled, and he stayed and defended it. Then he struck down the Philistines, and the LORD brought about a great victory.

One thousand sounds like a nice round number, and the verse stops short of it. The text says Josheb-basshebeth wields his spear against eight hundred men, whom he kills at one time. He's chief of the Three, and eight hundred is the number the writer gives.

Yes, the LORD. The verse says, "The LORD brought about a great victory that day." Eleazar stood his ground and struck the Philistines until his hand grew weary and stuck to his sword. Even so, the credit goes to the LORD.
Plunder, that's the word. The verse says the troops returned to Eleazar, "…but only to plunder the dead." They came back for that and nothing more. I have a feeling Eleazar's sticky hand noticed.

Right in the middle, baker. Shammah "…took his stand in the middle of the field…" (2 Samuel 23:12). The troops have fled, and he takes his stand anyway. Lentils all around his ankles, and he's not budging.
The verse doesn't mention a road. Shammah "…took his stand in the middle of the field…" (2 Samuel 23:12). That's where he is when he defends it and strikes down the Philistines.

Break through. The three mighty men "…broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well near the gate of Bethlehem, and brought it back to David." (2 Samuel 23:16). David only wished out loud, and they broke through a whole camp to answer it. I've had people bring me a drink of water, but never through a camp.
False is right. The three men bring the water back, and David "…refused to drink it…" (2 Samuel 23:16). He pours it out to the LORD instead. After all that effort, turning it down is the surprise.
David doesn't hand it back to the three. The verse says he refused to drink it and poured it out to the LORD (2 Samuel 23:16). The water goes to the LORD instead.

Joab it is. Abishai son of Zeruiah is the brother of Joab (2 Samuel 23:18), and Joab son of Zeruiah was over David's army (2 Samuel 8:16). Two brothers, both in David's story. That's a lot of family on one list.
Abner is a different man. He was the son of Ner and Saul's army commander (1 Samuel 14:50–51). The verse says Abishai is the brother of Joab, who was over David's army (2 Samuel 8:16).

Five hundred is a good guess, but the verse says three hundred. Abishai wields his spear against three hundred men and wins a name along with the Three (2 Samuel 23:18). Eight hundred, three hundred, five hundred, I lose count of a cookie batch at twelve, so these numbers have me dizzy.
The verse doesn't say wolf. Benaiah goes down into a pit on a snowy day and kills a lion (2 Samuel 23:20). A pit, snow and a lion in one verse, and I'd have turned around at the snow.

That's it! Benaiah "…snatched the spear from his hand, and killed the Egyptian with his own spear." (2 Samuel 23:21). The Egyptian had a spear in his hand, and Benaiah went against him with a club. In the end, it was the Egyptian's own spear that settled it.

The text doesn't mention any help. It says Benaiah went against the Egyptian with a club, snatched the spear from his hand, and killed him with his own spear (2 Samuel 23:21). No one else is named in the fight.
